text.p: Salomon Brothers said in a report released on Wednesday that an early resolution of Digital Video Disk (DVD)-related issues might greatly enhance the 1997 profits of Zoran Corp.

But Salomon kept its rating for the company, whose products are used in audio and video multimedia, at "hold". It estimated earnings per share of $0.70 in 1997 and $1.20 in 1998, up from $0.42 in 1996, as revenues double to $88 million.
"We believe that PC manufacturers and consumer electronic companies will introduce a whole range of products that utilise digital compression technology," Salomon said.

It said sales of compression products for consumer items like DVD players and PCs with DVD-ROM were expected to reach more than $500 million by 1999. The market for other, commercially available products like filmless digital cameras and video editing systems, would reach another $400-600 million.

"Zoran is attractively positioned to take advantage of these ...future opportunities," said analyst Victor Halpert, who estimated the company controls more than 70 percent of the video editing compression market.

Delay in introduction of PCs with DVD-ROM reflected limited availability of decryption chips and DVD-ROM drives and lack of licence approval to distribute decryption software. DVD players are available only in the Far East, mainly in Japan.
"Zoran remains a very attractive technological and market leader in multimedia compression. The early solution of DVD-related issues may greatly enhance the company's 1997 profitability."
